interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. VerifyLeader reports success although the leader can reach fewer voters than the voter quorum it sized, because acknowledgements arriving on non-voter replication streams are counted as support. Evidence from receipt 7a54f3754b0b423aaf1ba6c0365367c0 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the trigger: five members were bootstrapped, two were demoted to non-voters, and the leader's transport was disconnected in both directions from the two remaining voters, so voters_reachable=1 against quorum_voters=2 while nonvoters_reachable=2; VerifyLeader completed with verify_ok=true and an empty error, and the node was still Leader. Parsed index 3, the control on an identically built cluster with the non-voters also disconnected (nonvoters_reachable=0): the same call completed with verify_ok=false and the error 'leadership lost while committing log', the node by then a Follower. The two cases differ only in whether the non-voters could answer, so the successful verification in the trigger is attributable to non-voter acknowledgements rather than to voter support. Mechanism from source: verifyLeader sets quorumSize with quorumSize(), which counts only voters (raft.go:1087-1100), but registers the verify future on every entry of leaderState.replState (raft.go:966-990), and startStopReplication creates a replication state for every configured server including non-voters (raft.go:583-600); any successful heartbeat or AppendEntries response calls notifyAll(true) (replication.go:100-112), which increments the verify future's vote count (future.go:274-293) and completes it at the voter-sized quorum. The library already uses the correct supporter set one function away: checkLeaderLease iterates the latest configuration and counts only voters (raft.go:1037-1050), so the two paths disagree about who can establish leadership. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a client that calls VerifyLeader to protect a read (api.go:927-931) is told the leader still holds a voter quorum while it can reach none of the other voters, so the guard against serving stale reads after leadership loss does not hold in a cluster that contains non-voters. A successor run, receipt e49121154f514e39b6c1a37a2c353a4a, repeated the call every 50 ms after the first verification and quantified the window: parsed index 1 again records verify_ok=true for the partitioned leader, and parsed index 2 records loop_successes=20 with ms_until_failure=1015 before the node became a Follower, so twenty separate verifications succeeded across about one second; the control at parsed index 4 recorded verify_ok=false and parsed index 5 recorded loop_successes=0 with failure at 0 ms. The false assurance therefore lasts for the leader lease interval (LeaderLeaseTimeout, one second in this harness), not for a single call. A clean-copy repeat of the same fixed experiment, receipt 13b7844febba4a6d80c7331818c943f6, reproduced the window: parsed index 1 verify_ok=true, parsed index 2 loop_successes=20 with ms_until_failure=1014, parsed index 4 verify_ok=false and parsed index 5 loop_successes=0. Both runs therefore agree on the count and on a window of about one second at this lease setting. End-to-end consequence, measured in receipt 27d9e2e68fcf4e15b00b170ef9593714 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): five real nodes run as three voters and two non-voters with a recording state machine, the leader commits v1, is partitioned from the other two voters while the non-voters stay reachable, and is asked to verify itself immediately afterwards. Parsed index 0 records that state (voters_reachable=1, nonvoters_reachable=2, leader_value=v1); parsed index 1 records verify_after_partition_ok=true with ms_to_verify=0, so the false assurance is issued at once, but it also records ms_to_new_leader=2564 with new_leader_value=v2, verify_after_failover_ok=false and the error 'node is not the leader', old_value_before_heal=v1 against the successor's v2, and stale_verified_read=false. The old leader therefore stopped being able to verify itself before any successor had committed, so in this configuration the defect never became a verified stale read. Parsed index 3, the control with the non-voters also cut: verification failed after 1009 ms with 'leadership lost while committing log', and the successor committed v2 at 1476 ms, which shows the success in the trigger again depended on the non-voters while both cases ended with the old leader out of office. Second suffrage shape, receipt c211ca53de834d06a9b84e80fc18f1b7 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): four members, one of them demoted, so the configuration has three voters and exactly one non-voter and the voter quorum is two. Parsed index 0 records voters_reachable=1, nonvoters_reachable=1, quorum_voters=2, demotion_converged=true and demotion_converge_ms=5, so the member whose acknowledgement is being counted had already applied its own demotion; parsed index 1 records verify_ok=true in 0 ms with the node still Leader, although it could reach only one of the two voters its sizing requires. Parsed index 3, the control with the single non-voter also cut: verify_ok=false after 50 ms with 'leadership lost while committing log', the node a Follower. One non-voter is therefore enough to supply the acknowledgement the voter quorum is missing, and the success ends as soon as that member is unreachable. Why the window closes is structural rather than lucky: this library rejects a configuration whose LeaderLeaseTimeout exceeds its HeartbeatTimeout, and requires HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a follower cannot begin an election before the old leader's lease has already run out, and the vote round trip only adds to that margin. The defect's practical reach is therefore a false leadership-health signal that lasts up to one lease interval, not a stale read after a failover. The membership document defines a non-voter as 'a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes' (membership.md:11-12), which supports treating a non-voter's acknowledgement as ineligible support for a leadership verification sized as a voter quorum.

Repeat of the end-to-end experiment, receipt fb14e70f60a3456eae7774eb6e005e69 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same fixed inputs were run again. Parsed index 0 records the trigger's state with one of three voters and both non-voters reachable, and parsed index 1 its result: the leader verified itself at 0 ms after the partition, the successor was elected and applied the new value at 2373 ms, the old leader's own value was still the initial one before the heal, its later verification failed with 'node is not the leader', and no stale verified read was recorded. Parsed index 2 records the control's state with the non-voters unreachable as well, and parsed index 3 its result: verification failed after 994 ms with 'leadership lost while committing log', the successor applied the new value at 1917 ms, and again no stale verified read. The bound the account claims therefore reproduces on a second execution with a successor about 190 ms faster than in the first run, so the false success remains confined to the interval between the partition and the lease-driven step-down rather than being an artifact of one run's timing.

Lease variation, receipt 871eb51d712b4c269dd592937ab068f7 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same five-member shape with two non-voters and the leader cut from the two remaining voters, run at two lease settings. Parsed index 0 records the 500 ms case with a 500 ms heartbeat and a 600 ms election timeout, and parsed index 1 its result: the first verification succeeded at 0 ms, ten consecutive verifications succeeded, the first failure came at 510 ms and the leader ended as a follower. Parsed index 2 records the 1 s case with a 1 s heartbeat and a 1 s election timeout, and parsed index 3 its result: the first verification succeeded at 0 ms, twenty consecutive verifications succeeded, the first failure came at 1018 ms and the leader again ended as a follower. The window therefore follows the configured lease across a factor of two, roughly 510 ms against 1018 ms, which replaces the earlier inference from a single setting, and the number of successes scales with it as well, ten against twenty at a fifty-millisecond interval.

Question-level consolidation after the premise correction. The verification entry now records that verifyLeader starts the count at one for the leader itself, sizes a voter-only quorum and registers the future on every replication stream. Read across both lineages that this account uses, that arithmetic explains every recorded outcome: in the five-member receipts the quorum is two, the leader supplies one vote and a single non-voter acknowledgement completes the verification, and the control with the non-voters also cut has no second acknowledgement and fails after about a second; in the lease receipts the same shape succeeds at the first attempt under both a 500 ms and a 1 s lease and then fails when the lease-driven step-down arrives, at 510 ms and 1018 ms; in the end-to-end receipts the same first verification succeeds at 0 ms while the successor commits only after about 2.4 seconds, and the later verification is refused because the node is no longer the leader. Nothing above depends on the leader being excluded from the count, so the correction sharpens the mechanism without changing the conclusion that the verification is satisfied without a second voter.

Nothing above depends on the leader being excluded from the count, so the correction sharpens the mechanism without changing the conclusion that the verification is satisfied without a second voter.

1e9081120a23413eaaf020fffb085a1b-gap-0.explanation: The current explanation and the lease experiment, both of which this question-level account carries, assert only that a verification succeeds while one of three voters is reachable and the non-voters answer. With the leader's self-vote recorded, that is exactly a quorum of two met by the leader plus one non-voter acknowledgement, so the affected uses are confirmed rather than revised; their recorded comparison results stay violated.

1e9081120a23413eaaf020fffb085a1b-gap-1.explanation: The end-to-end receipts from 2fd5794c550141f7889f1530295d1294-experiment, 27d9e2e68fcf4e15b00b170ef9593714 and its repeat fb14e70f60a3456eae7774eb6e005e69, are cited in this question-level record. They recorded a first verification succeeding at 0 ms under the same three-voter quorum, which the corrected premise explains the same way, and a later verification refused because the node had stepped down; neither observation depended on how the two votes were supplied, so those receipts need no reinterpretation and the bound they measured stands.

knowledge.assertion: verifyLeader arms the verification with the leader's own vote, sizes the quorum by voters and registers the future on every replication stream, so with three voters one non-voter acknowledgement completes it.
checkLeaderLease counts only voters, unlike VerifyLeader.

counterevidence: The verification returns before the lease check steps the leader down, so the false success is bounded by the leader lease interval rather than permanent; in the control that same step-down produced the error the trigger avoided. Receipt 27d9e2e68fcf4e15b00b170ef9593714 measures the bound directly: verification succeeded at 0 ms after the partition, the successor committed at 2564 ms, and the post-failover verification failed because the node was no longer the leader. The repeat, receipt fb14e70f60a3456eae7774eb6e005e69, measured the same shape: verification at 0 ms, the successor's commit at 2373 ms, and the later verification refused. Receipt 871eb51d712b4c269dd592937ab068f7 measured the same shape at two leases: the first failure came at 510 ms under a 500 ms lease and at 1018 ms under a 1 s lease, so the bound scales with the setting rather than being fixed.

VerifyLeader returning nil installed no leader and returned no data; the harm needs a client that relies on it as the guard the documentation describes. The end-to-end case issued a state-machine read after a later verification, and that verification failed, so no read was served under a false assurance.

Non-voter reachability does show the leader is alive and connected, so a deployment that used VerifyLeader only as a liveness probe would not be affected; the code sizes a voter quorum, which makes quorum the stated intent.
The partition was modelled by removing in-memory transport routing in both directions between the leader and the voters, not by dropping packets or crashing members.

The election that removes the false leader is not slowed down: in the end-to-end case the successors were elected 1.5 s and 2.6 s after the cut, while the lease expired after about 1 s, so neither case approached an overlap between a successful verification and a stale state machine.

In both suffrage shapes the successful verification was issued while the non-voters were reachable and stopped once they were cut, so the result is about which acknowledgements the call accepts, not about the size of the cluster.
limitations: Two suffrage shapes were exercised, both with three voters: five members with two non-voters and four members with one non-voter, each with the leader cut from the other voters. Larger clusters, configurations where non-voters outnumber voters, and a non-voter whose heartbeat is the only one in flight were not tested.

The end-to-end case reads the state machine directly rather than through a client read protocol, and its timing bound is configuration-specific: with a one-second lease and staggered election timeouts of 1.1 s, 2 s and 3 s the successors were elected at 2.6 s and 1.5 s. The library validates LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a lease longer than an election is not expressible and the window cannot be widened that way; a slower election would widen the false-verification interval without changing the fact that the successor arrives after the lease. The repeat recorded successor commits at 2373 ms in the trigger and 1917 ms in the control, so the bound moved by a few hundred milliseconds between runs without changing the order of events.

The demotions completed before the partition in the single-non-voter case, where the demoted member's own view was read back and had converged in 5 ms; in the five-member receipts the members' views of the new configuration were not read back before the transport was cut.

The stale-read case covers one partition shape and one partition timing, applied after the leader has committed and settled. A partition that begins while a verification is already in flight, or a leader whose lease contact comes from a voter that is about to be deposed, was not exercised.

The exposure window is now measured at two lease settings, 500 ms and 1 s, and follows them; a 2 s setting was attempted and abandoned because the cluster helper's stability wait is shorter than the election timeout that setting implies, so the scaling above 1 s is untested, and every case keeps the non-voters reachable and the election timeout at or just above the lease.

interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a goroutine other than the main RPC loop, as the fast-path contract permits, races the node's term update: the term it decided to persist can land after a higher term already persisted by the main thread, leaving the node below a term it had adopted. The lower the node's persisted term falls below the current leader's, the more willing it becomes to accept an older leader's messages, and it then replaces an entry it had already applied at the higher term with that leader's entry. Evidence. Consequence, receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b: parsed index 1 records after_newer_term=4, after_stale_term=3, persisted_term=3 and the write sequence [1 1 2 4 3] (term_decreased=true); parsed index 3 records the stale term-3 request being accepted (stale_request_accepted=true), the log at index 4 becoming stale4 while the FSM still holds new4, index 5 applied from the stale history as stale5, and both applied and commit indexes at 5 (applied_entry_replaced=true). Frequency, three clean-copy runs of receipt f13b5528eeb44ca99621e36f1c0f1ff0-experiment. Receipt 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8: 200 concurrent attempts with no added store latency produced inversion_count=0 (parsed index 1, comparison holds), while the same 200 attempts with a uniform 0-2 ms delay added to every current-term write produced inversion_count=90 (parsed index 3, comparison violated). Receipt b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c repeated the pair: 0 inversions without delay and 97 with it. Receipt 0ca5ad7d5e8140febbfcf1311e199a4c changes the reading of the no-delay mode: with the same inputs it recorded inversion_count=2 without delay (parsed index 1) and 105 with jitter (parsed index 3). Concurrency alone therefore suffices, at a low rate, and the added 0-2 ms write delay raises that to roughly half of all attempts; the two earlier zero counts are consistent with a no-delay rate near one percent rather than with an impossibility. Delay sweep, receipt 1bec110248d14e9e80aac0f8b8129f1c (five cases, 200 attempts each, a fresh store, transport and raft per case): with a maximum current-term write delay of 0 us, parsed index 1 records inversion_count=0; at 250 us, parsed index 3 records 96; at 500 us, parsed index 5 records 95; at 1 ms, parsed index 7 records 100; at 2 ms, parsed index 9 records 94. Every comparison asserting zero inversions therefore holds in the zero-delay case and is violated at every other setting. The dependence on latency is not gradual: the rate jumps from none to about half between no delay and a quarter-millisecond maximum, and stays there across a further eightfold increase. A maximum of 250 us means a mean delay of 125 us before an in-memory write, which is the order of ordinary scheduling and syscall jitter rather than of an unusually slow disk. Mechanism from source: Transport documents the heartbeat handler as a fast-path (transport.go:58-64); NetworkTransport classifies an AppendEntries as a heartbeat exactly when the term is non-zero, a leader address is present, both previous-log fields are zero, no entries are carried and LeaderCommitIndex is zero - the shape the leader's heartbeat request builds (net_transport.go:660-690, replication.go:388-397) - and for that shape calls the registered handler directly on the connection-handler goroutine, skipping the consumer channel (net_transport.go:718-736), with NewRaft registering r.processHeartbeat (api.go:626-632). appendEntries tests a.Term above r.getCurrentTerm(), then calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term), which writes the stable store and afterwards stores the same value atomically without re-checking (raft.go:1470-1490, 2164-2172); the gap between the store write and the atomic store is where a concurrent higher-term writer can be overtaken. The subsequent acceptance and truncation run on the entry path that trusts the current term (raft.go:1526-1566). Consequence under the exercised conditions: a follower whose term write is overtaken by a concurrent heartbeat can finish below an already adopted term and then accept and apply a stale leader's conflicting entries, leaving its log and FSM describing different histories. The window needs no artificially delayed store and no large latency: a write that is merely a few tens of microseconds slower than the main thread's own write is enough for the inversion, and once the delay exceeds a quarter millisecond the race is as likely as not in this harness. The concurrency this depends on is a declared design choice: the target's divergence document states that it performs heartbeating concurrently with other AppendEntries RPCs 'to avoid having to set the election timeout high enough to account for the max acceptable disk operation' (docs/divergence.md:25-34), so the term update must remain correct under exactly this overlap. Real storage latency, receipt f87365ea88ba4a48a610ba8f380419b0 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same follower race with the synthetic delay replaced by a file write plus fsync on every current-term update. Parsed index 0 records the case with 200 attempts in mode file_write_plus_fsync; parsed index 1 records inversion_count=89, term_writes=402, mean_write_us=1993 and max_write_us=16202. The inversion therefore occurs under genuine file-system latency of the order a containerised deployment has, not only under an injected sleep, and the mean write duration sits in the range where the sweep showed the rate saturated.

Repeat of the same fixed experiment, receipt a20ffdbaf258403c8f0c6a4d4c141e1f (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the saved harness and inputs were executed again unchanged, giving a fourth pair of arms at 200 attempts each. Parsed index 0 records the no-delay case state with final_term 400 and max_delay_ms 0, and parsed index 1 its result with inversion_count 1. Parsed index 2 records the jittered case state with final_term 303 and max_delay_ms 2, and parsed index 3 its result with inversion_count 98. The no-delay counts are now 0, 0, 2 and 1 over four independent runs, so the inversion recurs without any added delay and the estimate no longer rests on a single run with two events; the jittered counts are 90, 97, 105 and 98, a band of fifteen events out of four hundred, so added delay remains a large amplifier rather than a precondition. Nothing else about the mechanism changes.

Repeat of the fsync arm, receipt ad511acf2fed45ae90f30f200ec3d4d1 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same fixed harness ran again with a file write plus fsync on every current-term update. Parsed index 0 records the case with 200 attempts in mode file_write_plus_fsync, and parsed index 1 its result: inversion_count 69, term_writes 402, mean_write_us 2452 and max_write_us 7223. Against the earlier run of the same harness, which recorded 89 inversions with a mean write near 2 ms and a maximum near 16 ms, the exposure reproduces at the same order of magnitude under genuine file-system latency, so the claim no longer rests on one execution; the rate varies with this container's storage behaviour, which is what the account already says a rate here is a property of the harness.

knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: Concurrency alone reaches the inversion, but rarely in this harness at zero delay: the four jitter-probe runs recorded 0, 0, 2 and 1 inversions in the 200 no-delay attempts each, and the sweep's zero-delay case recorded 0 in another 200, so three of eight hundred no-delay attempts inverted against ninety to one hundred and five of two hundred with jitter. A rate near one per cent with wide uncertainty is the reading of those counts, so the delay is an amplifier rather than a precondition and the zero-delay counts are small but recurrent.

The stale term-3 and newer term-4 requests are crafted AppendEntries whose leader commit indexes are asserted by the request, not produced by a quorum of live peers; only one real node ran in either receipt. The claim therefore rests on the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed, which the harness asserts rather than demonstrates.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 exists between the log and the FSM and would surface on a restart replay.

The sweep's saturation level is the probability that the heartbeat's write is still in flight when the higher-term write completes; in this harness that probability is near one half because the two writes start almost together. A deployment whose heartbeat and AppendEntries paths are not started concurrently would see a different level, and the harness did not vary the start offset.

A real file write plus fsync on every current-term update, receipt f87365ea88ba4a48a610ba8f380419b0, produced 89 inversions in 200 attempts with a mean write of 1.993 ms and a maximum of 16.2 ms, so the exposure does not depend on a synthetic sleep; the latency is still this container's filesystem rather than any particular deployment's storage stack. A second run of the same harness, receipt ad511acf2fed45ae90f30f200ec3d4d1, recorded 69 inversions in 200 attempts with a mean write of 2.45 ms and a maximum of 7.2 ms.
limitations: Two timing modes, 200 attempts each, run four times on one platform: the jittered case produced 90, 97, 105 and then 98 inversions, and the no-delay case produced 0, 0, 2 and then 1. These counts are properties of this harness's delay distribution and scheduler, not a field rate, and the no-delay estimate still rests on three events in eight hundred attempts, so it bounds the order of magnitude rather than the rate.

The two competing leaders were modelled by crafted requests over the real consumer path; the obsolete leader's partition, its continued heartbeating and the newer leader's quorum were not produced by real nodes, and repeated attempts reuse one node's log.
Only the term and leader writes of the fast-path were exercised; whether other concurrent fast-path effects interact with snapshot installation or configuration updates was not tested.

The sweep samples five maxima, 0, 250 us, 500 us, 1 ms and 2 ms, with a uniform delay from zero and one fresh node per setting. It shows that the rate is zero at no delay and already saturated at 250 us, but it does not locate the transition between those two points, and it does not test delays above 2 ms or a non-uniform distribution.
The fix boundary is unexamined: a compare-and-set term update would close this interleaving, but no protective mechanism in the captured code was tested against it.

The fsync arm has now run twice on one container filesystem, recording 89 and 69 inversions in 200 attempts with mean writes of about 2.0 and 2.5 ms; neither run varies the storage stack, the file system or the sync mode, so the reproduction shows stability of the exposure on this platform rather than a field rate.
interpretations.joint_history: All five receipts belong to this investigation and run the same follower-side setup; they answer different parts of the question. Receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b forces one interleaving with a held term write and measures what happens afterwards, while receipt 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8 repeats the race 200 times per timing mode without a hook and measures only the inversion count. Receipts b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c and 0ca5ad7d5e8140febbfcf1311e199a4c are clean-copy repeat executions of that frequency experiment; they add reproducibility and the second also shows that the no-delay mode is not perfectly clean. Receipt 1bec110248d14e9e80aac0f8b8129f1c comes from a separate experiment identifier, d6d15a60678d422d94174a2432cd3782-experiment, that turns the same race into a delay sweep: the attempt body, the request shapes and the inversion criterion are those of the frequency experiment, and the only differences are that the delay becomes a swept parameter and that each setting gets its own store, transport and raft. Receipt f87365ea88ba4a48a610ba8f380419b0 comes from a further experiment identifier, cc2661ee13b14149b7ca04c9d5a35509-experiment, which keeps the attempt body, request shapes and inversion criterion and changes only the source of the write latency: a real file write plus fsync instead of a sleep. Receipt a20ffdbaf258403c8f0c6a4d4c141e1f is a repeat execution of f13b5528eeb44ca99621e36f1c0f1ff0-experiment from its retained inputs, so its four events are the same cases, admissions and assertions as receipts 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8, b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c and 0ca5ad7d5e8140febbfcf1311e199a4c and differ only in the scheduler's behaviour during that run. Receipt ad511acf2fed45ae90f30f200ec3d4d1 is a repeat execution of cc2661ee13b14149b7ca04c9d5a35509-experiment from its retained inputs, so its case, admission and assertion match receipt f87365ea88ba4a48a610ba8f380419b0 and differ only in the storage timings of that run.

interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted without any refusal keyed to its suffrage and does not install that member as leader; the attempt instead forces an election round in which every member's term advances, leadership lands on a member the caller did not name, and leadership is absent for a measurable interval in the earlier five-member receipts, while the four-member receipt below recorded no leaderless sample. Evidence, five receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Parsed index 3 of both receipts, the trigger where one non-leader member was demoted with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with an empty future_error, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. A successor run, receipt 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d, corrects the earlier measurement: the target's own configuration is read after DemoteVoter returns and polled until it changes (demotion_converged=true, demotion_converge_ms=0), and at the moment the transfer is requested the target itself reports target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter, so the member's own view already showed it held no vote; it still campaigned (7 candidate samples, 7 leaderless samples, target_term_after=4, target_ever_leader=false, future_ok=true with an empty error) while the voter control at parsed index 1 installed the named target and produced 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples. In receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f the trigger produced 8 candidate samples with 8 leaderless samples (about 80 ms with no member reporting Leader) out of 470 samples at roughly 10 ms spacing, against 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471 in that run's control. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and all other members at 4, one step beyond the rejected round) and its leaderless interval match exactly that path, while the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Clean-copy repeat, receipt 3324fe87d6da49c6b53eab0e116823df (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): re-executing the corrected experiment from its retained inputs reproduced the pair. Parsed index 0, the voter control: target_role_in_own_config=voter, future_ok=true in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, and 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471. Parsed index 2, the trigger case: target_demoted=true, demotion_converged=true at 0 ms and target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter; parsed index 3: future_ok=true with an empty error in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, 6 candidate samples and 6 leaderless samples (about 60 ms) out of 470, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4. The corrected result is therefore observed twice with the target's own configuration confirming the non-voter role at request time. Demotion race, receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d (twenty attempts, each on a fresh four-voter cluster): the harness started DemoteVoter for a follower and immediately issued LeadershipTransferToServer for the same member, without waiting for the demotion to commit or for any voter to apply it. Parsed index 1 records demote_ok_count=20, transfer_ok_count=20, target_led_count=0, final_target_count=0 and target_ended_nonvoter=20, with no transfer error. Issuing the two requests back to back therefore cannot install a member whose vote is being removed: the transfer is admitted and reports success, and the election it provokes is still rejected because the voters' applied configuration decides the outcome. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member receives a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, an extra election round that raises every member's term, and a leaderless interval whose length follows the configured election timeout.

Entry-point comparison, receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): one four-member cluster per case, one follower demoted in each, and the demoted member's own configuration view reporting the non-voter role before the transfer, converging in 0 ms in the control and 6 ms in the trigger. Parsed index 0 records the control's state and parsed index 1 its result: the automatic LeadershipTransfer() needed one attempt, its future returned nil in 106 ms, leadership ended on a voter that is not the demoted member, no leaderless sample was seen in 26 samples over three seconds, and a client Apply and a GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. Parsed index 2 records the trigger's state and parsed index 3 its result: five attempts spanning 1035 ms each returned 'leadership transfer in progress', the named member never reported Leader across the same 26 samples, the final leader is a different voter, and the client Apply and GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. The control therefore shows that transfer works on this cluster shape and that the automatic path avoids the demoted member, while the explicit path admits the named member, keeps reporting a transfer in progress, and never installs it; both the earlier nil futures and this receipt's in-progress errors are consistent with the same gap, since neither is a refusal keyed to the target's lack of a vote.

Transfer-state probe, receipt 78769a572c5b4b249e441ac7ce63422a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same demote-then-transfer setup run twice with the leader's leadership-transfer flag sampled around each call. Parsed index 0 records the single-case state and parsed index 1 its result: the flag read false before the call, false as soon as the future was returned, false after the future completed and false three hundred milliseconds later; one attempt completed in 0 ms with no error, the named member never reported Leader across 283 samples over three seconds, no sample was leaderless, and the final leader is a different member. Parsed index 2 records the retry-case state and parsed index 3 its result: the flag read false before the first attempt, that attempt returned no error so the loop stopped after one, the named member never led across 284 samples, six samples were leaderless (about 60 ms), and the final leader is again a different member. Two things follow. The request was issued with no transfer already running and the library nevertheless accepted the demoted member as a target and reported the transfer as complete, so the earlier receipt's in-progress error is not evidence of a pre-existing transfer; and because the future succeeds while the named member never leads, the surface the caller sees is success, not a refusal, which is the form of the gap the account claims.

Repeat of the entry-point comparison, receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same fixed inputs were run again with no changes. Parsed index 0 records the control's state and parsed index 1 its result: one automatic attempt completed in 106 ms with no error, leadership ended on a voter that is not the demoted member, no leaderless sample was seen in 26 samples, and a client Apply and GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded in about 2 ms. Parsed index 2 records the trigger's state and parsed index 3 its result: the first attempt already returned 'leadership transfer in progress', all five attempts over 1036 ms returned the same error, the named member never reported Leader, the final leader is a different voter, and the post-transfer Apply and GetConfiguration both succeeded. The in-progress surface therefore reproduces exactly in this harness across two runs, with the same error, the same five attempts and the same roughly one-second span, so it is a stable property of this sequence rather than a one-off event; the flag probe's clean first call remains a different sequence, and the difference between them is not yet identified.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.

The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general. The repeat reproduced that control as well, with the named voter installed and no leaderless samples.

The measured disruption is small in absolute terms because the cluster ran with inmemConfig timeouts (Heartbeat/Election/Lease 50 ms): the three trigger runs recorded 8, 7 and 6 leaderless samples (about 80, 70 and 60 ms) and one extra election round, against zero leaderless samples in the voter controls. The interval follows the configured election timeout, so a production configuration of about 1 s would scale it accordingly; these millisecond figures are not a bound for other settings.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.

The nil-future surface is therefore reproducible in this harness across two runs, alongside the entry-point harness's reproducible in-progress surface and the flag probe's single clean call, so the account now holds two independently reproduced futures outcomes for the same request rather than one of each.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.

The control cases show the same mechanism transferring leadership correctly: the explicit transfer to an ordinary voter installed that named voter with a single term advance, and the later automatic control completed in about a hundred milliseconds with leadership on a voter and no leaderless samples. The defect is therefore specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general or to the entry-point harness's sequencing.

The measured disruption is small in absolute terms because the cluster ran with inmemConfig timeouts (Heartbeat/Election/Lease 50 ms): the three trigger runs recorded 8, 7 and 6 leaderless samples (about 80, 70 and 60 ms) and one extra election round, against zero leaderless samples in the voter controls. The interval follows the configured election timeout, so a production configuration of about 1 s would scale it accordingly; these millisecond figures are not a bound for other settings.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.

Both corrected runs show the target's own configuration had already converged to non-voter before the request, so the exercised case is a member that knew it could not win; a demoted member whose own view still lagged (a stale configuration) was not exercised, although the earliest runs exercised an unknown mix.

The demotion race is a negative result for elevation: in 20 attempts issued back to back, no target became leader and every transfer reported success, so the timing gap that could have produced a worse outcome did not do so in this harness.

The future's result is not uniform across receipts: the demotion race receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d recorded successful transfer futures in all twenty attempts, while receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b recorded 'leadership transfer in progress' on every one of five attempts on a four-member cluster whose demoted member's view had already converged. The sentence that the future completes without error therefore describes those receipts and not the operation in general, and the durable observation common to both is that the named member is never installed and no suffrage check refuses it. The repeat of the entry-point comparison, receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586, reproduced the in-progress surface exactly, with the same error on all five attempts over 1036 ms, so within that harness the surface is stable. A second run of the demotion race, receipt 334d7a88f3b244548f316bcdb42b779e, reproduced that surface, with twenty successful futures and no attempt in which the named member led.

The in-progress error seen in receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b is not reproduced here: with the transfer flag clear before the call, the same explicit request returned no error at all. The account therefore cannot claim that the error is a stable consequence of naming a non-voter, only that neither outcome is a refusal keyed to the target's suffrage and neither installs the target.
limitations: The cluster size is four members throughout, with three voters after the demotion, and the transfer always targets a non-leader member. The demotion race covers a transfer issued concurrently with the demotion, but a cluster whose only non-voter is the sole reachable member and a transfer that lands while the leader is already losing office to another election were not tested.

Leaderless counts are sampled every ~10 ms over roughly 4.7 s of the 5 s window (470 to 471 samples); a gap shorter than the sample spacing would be missed, so 60 to 80 ms is a lower bound for the trigger and the controls' zero does not prove uninterrupted leadership.

Only immediate convergence was observed in the corrected runs: the demoted member's own view reported the new role within the first poll (0 ms), so no single-case run exercised a target whose configuration still showed it as a voter at request time. The demotion race issues the transfer before applying, but it records the target's final role rather than its view at request time.
That the voter members had committed the demotion before the transfer is inferred from their rejection and term adoption, not from reading each voter's configuration.

Out of scope: whether an unprivileged or misconfigured peer could send TimeoutNow directly, even though timeoutNow performs no term, leader or membership check (raft.go:2232-2237); that path was not exercised here.

Three harnesses now give two reproduced and one single futures outcome for the same request: the demotion race returned successful futures in all twenty attempts on both of its runs, the entry-point harness returned 'leadership transfer in progress' on all five attempts on both of its runs, and the flag probe returned no error on its single run with the transfer flag clear. The difference between the flag probe and the other two therefore lies in their preceding steps, which include repeated leader and configuration polling before the transfer, and which of those steps sets the transfer state is not yet identified; all three keep the demoted member's own view reporting the non-voter role before the call.
interpretations.joint_history: All five receipts belong to this investigation. Receipts d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba, 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f and 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d are successive revisions of the same fixed experiment: the first run, a revision adding per-member state sampling, and the revision that reads the target's own configuration after the demotion. Receipt 334d7a88f3b244548f316bcdb42b779e is a repeat execution of cf5136d55dd74f22ad66c73229d55f35-experiment from its retained inputs, so its case, admissions and assertions match receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d.

interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated. With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft does not complete a legal replay of already-committed log entries once the replay needs more than 128 FSM dispatch batches; the caller never receives the *Raft, so the node has no way to start, serve or shut down. This is a startup progress failure, not a decision-safety failure: no commit, vote or membership decision was observed to be wrong. Evidence. Receipt d61420dbc49a4072937b040aac55a51c (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): parsed index 1, seeded commit-tracking store with 8192 committed entries = exactly 128 batches at MaxAppendEntries=64, returned=true in 5 ms; parsed index 3, the retained state of a real single-node cluster that committed 8300 commands through the leader/commit/apply path and then snapshotted at index 8302 above the staged commit index, replay 0 batches, returned=true in 0 ms; parsed index 5, the same seeded store with 8193 entries = 129 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with one newly blocked (*Raft).processLogs goroutine and one newly blocked (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs goroutine; parsed index 7, the same real-cluster prefix without a snapshot, staged commit 8300 = 130 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with the same two newly blocked goroutines. Successor receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0) reproduced all four outcomes (parsed indices 1, 3, 7, 9) and added parsed index 5: the identical 8193-entry store state that hangs at MaxAppendEntries=64, replayed as 9 batches with MaxAppendEntries=1024, returned=true in 2 ms. That comparison holds entry count, log content, staged commit index and snapshot state fixed and varies only the batch size, so the stall is attributable to the number of batches relative to the 128-slot channel rather than to log volume, snapshot handling, store state or the producing cluster; the goroutine match in both hanging cases localizes the block to processLogs invoked from restoreFromCommittedLogs. Mechanism from source: api.go:606 calls restoreFromCommittedLogs before any background goroutine exists; api.go:753 calls processLogs(commitIndex, nil); raft.go:1303-1313 sends each commitTuple batch into fsmMutateCh and selects only on that send and on r.shutdownCh; fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 (api.go:560); its only reader runFSM (fsm.go:241) is started at api.go:637 after NewRaft returns; api.go:1065 is the only closer of shutdownCh and is reachable only through a *Raft. After 128 successful sends the 129th send therefore has no producer and no possible closer, so the block is permanent rather than slow. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a node restarting with the documented RestoreCommittedLogs option and with more than 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond its last snapshot hangs inside NewRaft indefinitely while reporting no error. The operational restart path was measured separately in receipt f032fc49841048c9877653db9f877b27: a three-voter cluster committed 8400 commands, one follower accumulated them and staged its own commit index at 8400 with last log index 8402, and only that follower was restarted. With a snapshot taken on that follower at 8400 the replay was 0 batches and NewRaft returned in 0 ms (parsed index 1, comparison holds); without the snapshot the same follower needed 132 batches and NewRaft had not returned after 5000 ms (parsed index 3, comparison violated). The boundary therefore reproduces from the follower's own appendEntries-driven commit staging, not only from a feeding leader. The boundary was then checked at a second batch size: receipt f8b98d790cc14664af8af17775d3cc48 replays 131072 committed entries at MaxAppendEntries=1024, which is exactly 128 batches, and NewRaft returned in 45 ms (parsed index 7, comparison holds), while 131073 entries, one entry further and therefore 129 batches, did not return within 5000 ms (parsed index 9, comparison violated). The same capacity limit therefore governs a replay whose entry count is sixteen times larger, so the boundary follows the batch count rather than the default entry count. A third configuration point, receipt 14286fc183ac4bbc92a41f73a49a57d9 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0), moves the batch size to its smallest legal value: with MaxAppendEntries=1 the same product predicts a boundary of 128 entries. Parsed index 0 records replay_entries=128, replay_batches=128 and staged_commit_index=128; parsed index 1 records returned=true in 1 ms. Parsed index 2 records replay_entries=129 and replay_batches=129; parsed index 3 records returned=false after 5004 ms with the error 'no return within observation window', fsm_applied_sampled=0 and one new goroutine inside processLogs. The stated product 128*MaxAppendEntries therefore holds at 1, 64 and 1024, a span of 1024 in the entry count at which the block appears, and the smallest case shows the block needs no large volume of data, only one batch more than the channel can hold. A real-prefix case inside the shortened-replay region, receipt 7ee579ae94bd4812beaa21ce1ca9bb2e (completed, tests_passed, exit 0), commits 200 commands, takes a snapshot, commits a second batch and shuts down, so the restart replays only the tail after the snapshot. Parsed index 0 records snapshot_index=202, staged_commit_index=400, last_log_index=402, replay_entries=198 and replay_batches=4; parsed index 1 records returned=true in 3 ms. Parsed index 2 records the same first batch and snapshot with a second batch of 8300, giving staged_commit_index=8501, last_log_index=8502, replay_entries=8299 and replay_batches=130; parsed index 3 records returned=false after 5000 ms with one new goroutine inside processLogs. The recovery region between a zero-length replay and the blocked case is therefore observed on real prefixes rather than inferred: when the snapshot leaves four batches the constructor returns, and when it leaves 130 it does not. Permanence, receipt fd88bc508e4f413393838b7d64657137 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the seeded boundary pair at the default batch size, watched for longer than any earlier receipt. Parsed index 0 records 8192 entries and replay_batches=128 with a ten-second window; parsed index 1 records returned=true in 5 ms. Parsed index 2 records 8193 entries and replay_batches=129 with a thirty-second window; parsed index 3 records returned=false after 30000 ms with one new goroutine inside processLogs. The blocked case therefore outlasts the control's completion by roughly five thousand times, which is evidence of a permanent stall rather than a slow replay, and the source-level argument about the absent consumer and the unreachable closer is no longer the only ground for that claim.

Boundary measured on cluster-produced prefixes, receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): three restarts of retained single-node prefixes produced the same way, each committing 200 commands, snapshotting at index 202, committing a second batch and shutting down, so the replay is exactly the tail after the snapshot. Parsed index 0 records replay_entries=3199 and replay_batches=50 with staged_commit_index=3401 and last_log_index=3402; parsed index 1 records returned=true in 4 ms. Parsed index 2 records replay_entries=8192, replay_batches=128, staged_commit_index=8394 and last_log_index=8396; parsed index 3 records returned=true in 2 ms. Parsed index 4 records replay_entries=8194, replay_batches=129, staged_commit_index=8396 and last_log_index=8397; parsed index 5 records returned=false after 20000 ms with one new goroutine inside processLogs and new_blocked_process=1. The last pair shares the producing prefix shape and differs by one committed entry, so the return at 128 batches and the stall at 129 cannot be attributed to replay volume, snapshot size or the producing cluster, and the fifty-batch case measures the middle of the recovery region on real prefixes instead of a seeded store.

Repeat of the real-prefix boundary, receipt 791d25b96017428eb74a6280f460203e (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same three prefixes ran again with no changes. Parsed index 0 records the fifty-batch case with replay_entries=3199, replay_batches=50, staged_commit_index=3401 and last_log_index=3402, and parsed index 1 its result, returned=true in 2 ms. Parsed index 2 records replay_entries=8192 and replay_batches=128 with staged_commit_index=8394, and parsed index 3 its result, returned=true in 5 ms. Parsed index 4 records replay_entries=8194 and replay_batches=129 with staged_commit_index=8396, and parsed index 5 its result, returned=false after 20000 ms with one new goroutine inside processLogs. The pair that differs by a single committed entry therefore behaves the same way on a second execution, with the same 20 s block and the same parked goroutine, so the account's boundary no longer rests on a single run of the real-prefix harness.

knowledge.assertion: NewRaft calls restoreFromCommittedLogs synchronously and processLogs flushes batches into fsmMutateCh while runFSM starts only after NewRaft returns.
The startup replay can enqueue at most 128 batches, so 128*MaxAppendEntries replayed entries is the boundary beyond which no progress path exists.

counterevidence: RestoreCommittedLogs is not part of DefaultConfig (config.go:329-341 leaves it false), and with the option disabled restoreFromCommittedLogs returns immediately (api.go:725-727), so default-configured nodes cannot reach the blocked path.

A snapshot at or near the commit index removes the replay entirely: parsed index 3 in receipt d61420dbc49a4072937b040aac55a51c and the short case of receipt 7ee579ae94bd4812beaa21ce1ca9bb2e restarted real prefixes with a small enough tail that NewRaft returned, so snapshot cadence bounds exposure to this path. The repeat of the capacity pair, receipt 791d25b96017428eb74a6280f460203e, returned in 5 ms at 128 batches and did not return within 20 s at 129.

A larger MaxAppendEntries moves the boundary: parsed index 5 of receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a completed the very state that hangs at the default batch size, so a deployment that raises MaxAppendEntries enough for 128*MaxAppendEntries to cover its snapshot lag does not encounter the block.

The trigger observations are bounded windows, now including a thirty-second one in receipt fd88bc508e4f413393838b7d64657137 and a twenty-second one in receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633, but still finite runs; permanence is claimed from the source-level absence of any consumer before NewRaft returns, from shutdownCh having no closer outside Shutdown on the returned *Raft, and from the blocked cases outlasting the 128-batch controls' two-to-five-millisecond completions by four orders of magnitude.
No incorrect commit, applied entry, vote or membership decision was observed in any case; the evidence contradicts only startup progress.
limitations: The boundary is 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond the last snapshot, and it was exercised at three batch sizes: at 1 the boundary is 128 entries (129 blocked, 128 returned), at 64 it is 8192 entries (8193 blocked, 8192 returned) and at 1024 it is 131072 entries (131073 blocked, 131072 returned). Only three points were sampled, all with one entry per batch unit or a whole multiple of it, and the 128-slot fsmMutateCh capacity is not configurable, so no case varied it.

The seeded cases supply the commit-tracking store state directly. Eight restarts rest on a real prefix: a single-node leader (staged commit 8300, last log 8302, because the leader stages the pre-dispatch commit index), a three-voter cluster follower in both the snapshot and no-snapshot cases (staged commit 8400, last log 8402), the mid-run-snapshot prefixes at staged commits 400 and 8501 over a snapshot at 202, and three more from receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633 that also snapshot at 202 with staged commits 3401, 8394 and 8396.

The shortened-replay region is now sampled on real prefixes at four, fifty, 128, 129 and 130 batches, so the middle of it no longer rests on a seeded case; the pair at 128 and 129 holds batch size and prefix shape fixed and varies only the tail by one entry, while the batch-size variation still comes from the seeded cases at 1 and 1024. That pair has now been run twice with the same outcome, 5 ms at 128 batches and no return within 20 s at 129 in the second run.

fsm_applied_sampled is one sample at the end of each window and was 0 in every case, including the returning controls where runFSM had not yet applied anything, so it is not used as evidence of completion.

Out of scope here: whether the installSnapshot and restoreUserSnapshot sends to the same channel can block indefinitely on a running node, where runFSM is already active and would provide backpressure rather than a permanent block.

The longest observation is thirty seconds, and the real-prefix trigger of receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633 was watched for twenty. A replay that would eventually complete after that remains indistinguishable from one that never completes, although controls of the same shape finish in milliseconds and the goroutine remains parked in processLogs throughout.
interpretations.joint_history: Receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a is the successor of 1255b78953904846987cdc19826340c8-experiment under the same investigation: it retains the four case names, admissions and assertions unchanged, adds one case, and changes only the recorded max_append_entries field and the new case. The four retained result events agree with the earlier receipt (both controls returned, both triggers did not), so they describe the same subject. Receipt f8b98d790cc14664af8af17775d3cc48 is the next revision of that experiment and adds the MaxAppendEntries=1024 pair; its retained cases reproduce the earlier outcomes exactly. Receipt 14286fc183ac4bbc92a41f73a49a57d9 comes from a separate experiment identifier, 49133fbf233a47c287e4644facc4af06-experiment, built to sample the same product at MaxAppendEntries=1 with the same store, option and observation method. Receipt 7ee579ae94bd4812beaa21ce1ca9bb2e comes from another experiment identifier, f384564035f6401092ef5f875df0039c-experiment, built to restart real prefixes whose snapshot shortens the replay; it builds the prefix the same way as the earlier real-prefix cases (a single-node cluster applying commands through the leader and shutting down) and differs only in taking the snapshot between two batches and in recording the snapshot index and replay arithmetic in its own case and result events. Receipt fd88bc508e4f413393838b7d64657137 comes from a further experiment identifier, b102367291764616af9286671400ed39-experiment, which keeps the seeded boundary pair at the default batch size and only lengthens the trigger's observation window to thirty seconds; it adds a permanence measurement rather than a different state. Receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633 comes from a further experiment identifier, 3ba6c806449c483190a5cb2051f1ebc0-experiment, which builds its prefixes through the same production path as f384564035f6401092ef5f875df0039c-experiment and differs in the second-batch size, so its cases extend that experiment's four- and 130-batch real prefixes into the region between them and onto the boundary itself. Receipt 791d25b96017428eb74a6280f460203e is a repeat execution of 3ba6c806449c483190a5cb2051f1ebc0-experiment from its retained inputs, so its three cases, admissions and assertions match receipt 5298e93f6b814e72be0a4b16cfb10633.

interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted without any refusal keyed to its suffrage and does not install that member as leader; the attempt instead forces an election round in which every member's term advances, leadership lands on a member the caller did not name, and leadership is absent for a measurable interval in the earlier five-member receipts, while the four-member receipt below recorded no leaderless sample. Evidence, five receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Parsed index 3 of both receipts, the trigger where one non-leader member was demoted with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with an empty future_error, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. A successor run, receipt 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d, corrects the earlier measurement: the target's own configuration is read after DemoteVoter returns and polled until it changes (demotion_converged=true, demotion_converge_ms=0), and at the moment the transfer is requested the target itself reports target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter, so the member's own view already showed it held no vote; it still campaigned (7 candidate samples, 7 leaderless samples, target_term_after=4, target_ever_leader=false, future_ok=true with an empty error) while the voter control at parsed index 1 installed the named target and produced 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples. In receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f the trigger produced 8 candidate samples with 8 leaderless samples (about 80 ms with no member reporting Leader) out of 470 samples at roughly 10 ms spacing, against 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471 in that run's control. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and all other members at 4, one step beyond the rejected round) and its leaderless interval match exactly that path, while the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Clean-copy repeat, receipt 3324fe87d6da49c6b53eab0e116823df (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): re-executing the corrected experiment from its retained inputs reproduced the pair. Parsed index 0, the voter control: target_role_in_own_config=voter, future_ok=true in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, and 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471. Parsed index 2, the trigger case: target_demoted=true, demotion_converged=true at 0 ms and target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter; parsed index 3: future_ok=true with an empty error in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, 6 candidate samples and 6 leaderless samples (about 60 ms) out of 470, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4. The corrected result is therefore observed twice with the target's own configuration confirming the non-voter role at request time. Demotion race, receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d (twenty attempts, each on a fresh four-voter cluster): the harness started DemoteVoter for a follower and immediately issued LeadershipTransferToServer for the same member, without waiting for the demotion to commit or for any voter to apply it. Parsed index 1 records demote_ok_count=20, transfer_ok_count=20, target_led_count=0, final_target_count=0 and target_ended_nonvoter=20, with no transfer error. Issuing the two requests back to back therefore cannot install a member whose vote is being removed: the transfer is admitted and reports success, and the election it provokes is still rejected because the voters' applied configuration decides the outcome. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member receives a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, an extra election round that raises every member's term, and a leaderless interval whose length follows the configured election timeout.

Entry-point comparison, receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): one four-member cluster per case, one follower demoted in each, and the demoted member's own configuration view reporting the non-voter role before the transfer, converging in 0 ms in the control and 6 ms in the trigger. Parsed index 0 records the control's state and parsed index 1 its result: the automatic LeadershipTransfer() needed one attempt, its future returned nil in 106 ms, leadership ended on a voter that is not the demoted member, no leaderless sample was seen in 26 samples over three seconds, and a client Apply and a GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. Parsed index 2 records the trigger's state and parsed index 3 its result: five attempts spanning 1035 ms each returned 'leadership transfer in progress', the named member never reported Leader across the same 26 samples, the final leader is a different voter, and the client Apply and GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. The control therefore shows that transfer works on this cluster shape and that the automatic path avoids the demoted member, while the explicit path admits the named member, keeps reporting a transfer in progress, and never installs it; both the earlier nil futures and this receipt's in-progress errors are consistent with the same gap, since neither is a refusal keyed to the target's lack of a vote.

Transfer-state probe, receipt 78769a572c5b4b249e441ac7ce63422a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same demote-then-transfer setup run twice with the leader's leadership-transfer flag sampled around each call. Parsed index 0 records the single-case state and parsed index 1 its result: the flag read false before the call, false as soon as the future was returned, false after the future completed and false three hundred milliseconds later; one attempt completed in 0 ms with no error, the named member never reported Leader across 283 samples over three seconds, no sample was leaderless, and the final leader is a different member. Parsed index 2 records the retry-case state and parsed index 3 its result: the flag read false before the first attempt, that attempt returned no error so the loop stopped after one, the named member never led across 284 samples, six samples were leaderless (about 60 ms), and the final leader is again a different member. Two things follow. The request was issued with no transfer already running and the library nevertheless accepted the demoted member as a target and reported the transfer as complete, so the earlier receipt's in-progress error is not evidence of a pre-existing transfer; and because the future succeeds while the named member never leads, the surface the caller sees is success, not a refusal, which is the form of the gap the account claims.

Repeat of the entry-point comparison, receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same fixed inputs were run again with no changes.
